name: Snow load
seoTitle: Snow load Calculator: Free, With Steps
seoDesc: Snow load: work out snow type from the roof length and the roof width. A free construction calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: Give the Snow load calculator the roof length, the roof width, the snow cover thickness and the snow load and it returns snow type. It is built for a materials order or a planning estimate you want to get roughly right first time. The unit chips sit next to the boxes, which is where most hand-calculation mistakes start.

sections.title: How does the Snow load calculator work?
sections.html:
The Snow load calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports snow type in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the country, the state and the city); then you type in the roof length, the roof width, the snow cover thickness and the snow load.

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Snow load calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Snow type=(20000000 ÷ 196131) × snow load ÷ snow cover thickness
Maximum load=(roof pitch, state, city, (terrain type, roof exposure), temperature in the building, building importance, ground snow load, ground snow load)
Roof pitch (x:12)=(3 ÷ 5000000) × the square root of (-400000000000000 + 38467369161 × (total snow weight ^ 2) ÷ ((roof length ^ 2) × (roof width ^ 2) × (snow load ^ 2)))
Exposure factor=(terrain type, roof exposure)
Roof pitch (x:12)=12 × the tangent of (roof pitch)
Maximum snow cover thickness=((4000000000 ÷ 819239187) × (roof pitch, state, city, (terrain type, roof exposure), temperature in the building, building importance, ground snow load, ground snow load) ÷ snow type)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Snow load calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Quoting a job where areas and quantities drive the price
  • Checking a supplier's figure against your own measurements
  • Ordering material and not wanting a second trip
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the roof length, the roof width and the snow cover thickness — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Snow load calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns snow type, derived from the roof length, the roof width and the snow cover thickness. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Snow load calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the roof length, the roof width, the snow cover thickness and the snow load, which is 32 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter roof length in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Roof length opens in meters and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (28 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Roof pitch = 0 deg. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Snow load calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
